passage: Arnab and Jomon had been together four years when they signed the lease on a flat in Bengaluru. The first month went fine until the electricity bill came. Arnab had paid it without asking. Jomon felt oddly hurt. "It's not about the money," he said. "It's that we never decided." So on Sunday they sat on the floor with laptops and coffee. They listed income, rent and savings goals. Jomon wanted to save for his parents' house repairs; Arnab wanted to travel. They agreed on a shared account for household costs, split by income, and kept separate money for their own plans. They also agreed who handled which chores. It wasn't romantic. But both of them slept better that night.

qa.q: Where did Arnab and Jomon sign a lease?
qa.a: They signed a lease on a flat in Bengaluru.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel hurt when Arnab paid the bill?
qa.a: He felt left out of a decision about their shared life, not upset about the money itself.

qa.q: What did the couple agree on that could help other couples?
qa.a: A shared account for household costs split by income, separate money for personal plans, and clear chore roles.

qa.q: What would change if they had never had the Sunday talk?
qa.a: Small unspoken decisions might keep causing hurt and quiet resentment between them.

grounding: Shows a couple moving in together and negotiating shared finances, values and roles.

"Naveen-da, how did you know Ritu was the one?"
"Ramesh, that's a film question."
"I'm serious. Ma keeps sending profiles. One girl seems nice, but I don't know."
"What don't you know?"
"If we want the same things. She wants to live abroad. I want to stay near Ma."
"Did you ask her about it?"
"Not directly. It felt too early."
"Too early is better than too late. Ritu and I talked about money, kids, where to live, even who cooks. Before the engagement."
"Wasn't that awkward?"
"Very. We fought once. But after that I trusted her more."
"So I should just ask."
"Ask. And listen. Maybe she has good reasons."

qa.a: She wants to live abroad.

qa.q: What is Ramesh worried about?
qa.a: Ramesh is worried that the girl and Ramesh may want different things, since she wants to live abroad and Ramesh wants to stay near Ma.

qa.q: What advice does Naveen give Ramesh?
qa.a: Ask her directly about big things like money, children and where to live, and really listen to her reasons.

qa.q: How did talking early affect Naveen's relationship with Ritu?
qa.a: It was awkward and led to a fight, but afterwards Naveen trusted Ritu more.

passage: When Darshan and I got married two years ago, I assumed we'd share everything fifty-fifty. Then his father fell ill, and suddenly Darshan was travelling to Surat every weekend. I was cooking, working and paying most bills. I didn't say anything for months. I just got quieter and more irritable. One night I snapped over an unwashed pan. Darshan looked at me and said, 'Jasleen, this isn't about the pan, is it?' It wasn't. We talked until late. He hadn't noticed how much I was carrying; I hadn't told him how scared I was of becoming someone I resented. We changed things. He started planning meals on weekdays. I stopped pretending I was fine. Equal isn't always half-half. It has to be talked about.

qa.q: Where did Darshan travel every weekend?
qa.a: He travelled to Surat every weekend.

qa.q: What was Jasleen feeling during the months of silence?
qa.a: Jasleen felt overburdened and increasingly resentful, which showed as irritability rather than words.

qa.q: What helped the couple rebalance their roles?
qa.a: Talking honestly about what each was carrying and changing tasks, like Darshan planning weekday meals.

qa.q: How might Darshan have seen the situation before that night?
qa.a: He was focused on his ill father and didn't notice how much extra Jasleen was carrying.

grounding: Shows a married couple renegotiating roles and sharing responsibilities after a family change.

passage:
Pre-marriage counselling notes, session three (couples counsellor):
Keerthana, 25, and Sahil, 26, came in having argued over a joint account. Sahil assumed they would pool everything; Keerthana wanted to keep part of her salary separate, as she sends money to her mother each month. Sahil looked hurt, arms folded, and asked, 'Don't you trust me?' Keerthana answered quietly that it wasn't about trust; it was about her promise to her mother. I asked each to describe what money meant in their families growing up. Sahil's parents shared everything; Keerthana's mother had once had no money of her own. Both softened visibly. They drafted a plan: a joint account for shared costs, personal accounts for each, and her monthly transfer as an agreed item. We also listed who cooks, who handles bills, and whether they will live near his parents. Next session: careers, and children if they want them.

qa.q: Why does Keerthana want to keep part of her salary separate?
qa.a: She sends money to her mother every month.

qa.q: What did Sahil's folded arms and 'Don't you trust me?' suggest he felt?
qa.a: Hurt, because he read her wish for separate money as distrust.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help them move past the argument?
qa.a: By asking about money in their families growing up, which revealed the reasons behind each view before they drafted a practical plan.

qa.q: How might Keerthana's mother be affected by the couple's plan?
qa.a: Her monthly support stays secure as an agreed item, which spares her worry.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows a couple negotiating how to merge finances, values and household roles before marriage.

passage:
Sunday night
Sonali and I finally had the moving-in talk today, at the café by the lake: three hours and two pots of tea. I thought it would be romantic. It was mostly logistics, and I loved it anyway. What we agreed: rent split by income, not fifty-fifty, since she earns more and insisted. Cooking on alternate days; she hates washing up, so that's mine, and the bathroom is hers. We both want a dog someday, not yet. The hard part: my parents still don't know about us. She didn't push. She said she'd wait until I'm ready but doesn't want to hide forever. Fair. I told her I'll speak to Didi first, then Mummy. I'm scared, honestly. But writing the list made our life feel real, like something we're building, not just falling into.
— Mehak

qa.q: How did Mehak and Sonali agree to split the rent?
qa.a: By income, not fifty-fifty, since Sonali earns more.

qa.q: How does Mehak feel about telling the parents about Sonali?
qa.a: Scared, although Mehak has a plan to speak to Didi first and then Mummy.

qa.q: What made their conversation a good basis for living together?
qa.a: They talked openly about money, chores, future wishes and family, and agreed on concrete arrangements instead of assuming.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel about waiting for Mehak to tell her family?
qa.a: Patient but with limits; she respects Mehak's timing while not wanting to hide forever.

grounding: A diary entry shows a couple planning to live together by negotiating money, chores and family openness.

passage: In the courtyard of Yash's family home outside Udaipur, the wedding tent poles were already stacked against the wall. Damini sat with Yash on the charpai while his mother made tea inside. "Before the pheras," Damini said quietly, "I want us to agree on some things." Yash nodded. "Say it." "I'm keeping my job at the school. It's twelve kilometres; I'll take the bus." "Of course." "And your mother expects me to do the cooking alone." Yash was quiet. "She did it alone for thirty years." "I know. That's why I don't want to." He looked at the kitchen door. "I'll cook mornings, you evenings. And I'll tell Ma myself, not you." Damini let out a breath. "And money?" "Your salary is yours to decide. The house costs we talk about together." Inside, his mother laughed at something on the radio. Damini found she was smiling too.

qa.q: How far is the school where Damini will keep working?
qa.a: Twelve kilometres.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when she let out a breath?
qa.a: Damini felt relieved that Yash agreed and offered to speak to his mother himself.

qa.q: Why was it wise to agree on these things before the wedding?
qa.a: Settling work, chores and money early avoids hidden resentment later and shows how each will handle family pressure.

qa.q: How might Yash's mother see the new arrangement?
qa.a: She may feel surprised or unsettled, having cooked alone for thirty years, but hearing it from her son may help her accept it.

grounding: Before their wedding in a Rajasthan village, a couple agrees on work, chores and money roles.

passage: Aiko and Tuan had been together three years in Melbourne when her lease ended and they decided to move in together. Tuan found a flat in Footscray near his cousins; Aiko liked one by the sea in St Kilda. On a Sunday at the laundromat, watching their sheets spin, they did something they had never done: each listed what they needed. Aiko: quiet mornings, a window, weekends free to travel. Tuan: space to host his family for Tết, sending money to his parents in Huế every month, and never arguing about it. Aiko paused on the last one. She had assumed they would pool everything. "Is that a problem?" Tuan asked. "No," she said slowly. "I just need to know it's planned, so I'm not surprised." They chose a flat halfway, with a big kitchen, and agreed to sit down once a month to look at shared costs.

qa.q: Where did Tuan find a flat?
qa.a: In Footscray, near his cousins.

qa.q: What was Aiko feeling when she paused on Tuan's last need?
qa.a: Aiko felt a little surprised and uncertain, having assumed they would pool everything.

qa.q: What made the laundromat conversation a good way to decide?
qa.a: Listing each person's needs openly brought hidden expectations to the surface, leading to a compromise flat and monthly money talks.

qa.q: How might Tuan feel when Aiko says it isn't a problem?
qa.a: Tuan was probably relieved that his family support was respected, since he wanted to avoid arguing about it.

grounding: A couple in Australia move in together by openly listing needs, including family money commitments.

passage:
The pre-marriage workshop at the community hall had one strange exercise: each partner got a sheet with twenty household jobs and had to write who they imagined doing each one.

Deepika filled hers in quickly. Vishal took longer. When the facilitator asked them to swap, Deepika laughed, then stopped.

On Vishal's sheet, she had cooking, cleaning, his parents' medicines and "managing the maid". He had taken bills and the car.

"You've given me the whole house," she said quietly.

Vishal went red. "I didn't think. That's just how it is at my parents' place."

"I'll be working the same hours as you."

He looked at the list again. "Okay. What if we each take cooking three days a week? And medicines, that's my parents, so it's mine."

They spent the rest of the session crossing out and rewriting. By the end, both sheets were messy, and Deepika was smiling again.

qa.q: How many household jobs were on each sheet?
qa.a: Each sheet had twenty household jobs.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she saw Vishal's sheet?
qa.a: Deepika felt hurt and taken aback, seeing that he imagined her doing almost all the housework though she would work the same hours.

qa.q: How did the couple handle the mismatch well?
qa.a: They named the difference openly, Vishal admitted it came from his parents' home, and they rewrote the list together into a fairer split.

qa.q: How might Vishal have felt when the sheets were swapped?
qa.a: Vishal felt embarrassed, going red, as he realised he had copied his parents' pattern without thinking.

grounding: At a pre-marriage workshop, a couple discovers unequal assumptions about household roles and negotiates a fairer shared life.

passage:
Dear Zeenat,

I'm writing this instead of saying it, because every time we talk about money at dinner, one of us ends up clearing plates very loudly.

Here is what I think I understand. You want to keep sending something to your parents every month, because your father's pension is small. I grew up in a house where everything went into one account and my father decided. I don't want that for us, either.

I was hurt last week when you said I "count every rupee". I'm scared of us being careless, not of your parents.

Can we sit down on Sunday, with tea, not at dinner? Each of us writes what matters most: your parents, my savings goal, the flat. Then we work out a shared plan together, and if we get stuck, we see someone qualified who can help couples plan.

I love the life we're building. I want us to build it on purpose.

Hrithik

qa.q: Why does Zeenat want to keep sending something home each month?
qa.a: Because Zeenat's father's pension is small.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel on hearing the words "count every rupee"?
qa.a: Hrithik felt hurt, and explains that the worry comes from fear of being careless, not from resenting Zeenat's parents.

qa.q: What could make the Sunday talk work well?
qa.a: Choosing a calm time, having each person write their priorities first, and agreeing to see a qualified adviser if they get stuck.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Zeenat might feel relieved that Hrithik respects the duty to Zeenat's parents, and more willing to talk calmly now that Hrithik's fear is out in the open.

grounding: A young adult writes to a partner to negotiate shared finances and family values calmly, respecting both their priorities.

You asked me why I didn't marry the boy my parents found, Parveen. So here's the honest version from me, Pallavi, not the good-daughter version I tell aunties.

He was lovely on paper. Good job, good family. But on our third meeting, I mentioned I wanted to keep working after children, and he said, "We'll see." Just that. We'll see.

Then I met Aniket at the library where we both volunteer. What made me sure wasn't romance, though there was some. It was watching him cook for his sister when she was ill. It was that when I said I wanted to keep my job, he asked, "Which city would help your career more?"

We still argued, before the wedding, about whose parents we'd live near. We agreed on neither, a flat halfway, and visiting both on alternate Sundays.

My mother cried for a week. Now she calls Aniket more than she calls me.

qa.q: Where did Pallavi meet Aniket?
qa.a: She met Aniket at the library where they both volunteer.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the first match said "We'll see"?
qa.a: Pallavi felt uneasy and let down, sensing that her wish to keep working was not really respected.

qa.q: Which choices in Pallavi's story helped her choose a partner wisely?
qa.a: She watched how each man treated family and her ambitions, not just their profile, and settled a real conflict about where to live before the wedding.

qa.q: How did Pallavi's mother see the choice, then and later?
qa.a: At first her mother was upset and cried for a week, but later she grew fond of Aniket and now calls him often.

passage:
I'm Gopika. I shared a flat with Simran until she got engaged, and I heard more of their planning than I meant to.
One night, Simran and her fiancé Rehan sat at our dining table with a notebook and chai. They weren't arguing, but it wasn't romantic either. They talked about money: whose parents they'd each support, whether to have a joint account, what happens if one of them loses a job. Then chores: Rehan said he'd cook if Simran handled bills. Simran said, "Let's rotate. I don't want to be the bill person forever."
At one point Simran went very quiet. Rehan had said his mother expected them to live with her. They talked about it for an hour.
I don't know everything they felt. But when they got up, they'd written "decide by March" next to that line, and Simran was smiling.

qa.q: What did they write next to the line about living with Rehan's mother?
qa.a: "Decide by March."

qa.q: What does Simran going very quiet suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Simran felt surprised and uneasy on hearing Rehan's mother expected them to live with her.

qa.q: What made their planning conversation healthy?
qa.a: They discussed money, family support, chores and living arrangements openly before marriage, and gave the hardest question time instead of forcing it.

qa.q: Why might Gopika be careful about saying what they felt?
qa.a: Gopika was only overhearing from the flat, so Gopika could see their actions but not know their inner thoughts.

grounding: Illustrates, through a flatmate, a young couple negotiating finances, roles and values before marriage.

passage:
Monday: Kishore saw a transfer on the joint account: Rekha had sent money to her parents for her father's treatment. He hadn't known. He snapped, "You could have told me." Rekha snapped back, "You send money to your brother every month."
Wednesday: Neither spoke much. Kishore felt hurt; Rekha felt judged. They both slept badly.
Saturday: Rekha suggested they sit down properly. They wrote out what each sent to family and why, and discovered they both felt the same duty and hadn't said it aloud. They agreed on three things: talk before any big transfer, keep some money each could use without asking, and review together every month.
Rekha said, "I wasn't hiding it. I was scared you'd say no."
Kishore said, "I wasn't angry about the money. I was angry at not knowing."
They went for dinner afterwards, the first time that week.

qa.q: What was Rekha's transfer for?
qa.a: Her father's treatment.

qa.q: Why did Kishore feel hurt about the transfer?
qa.a: Kishore felt hurt and left out, because he wasn't angry about the money but about not being told.

qa.q: What made their Saturday conversation productive?
qa.a: They wrote out each person's family support, said their real feelings aloud, and agreed simple rules together.

qa.q: How did Rekha experience Kishore's reaction on Monday?
qa.a: Rekha felt judged and scared he would refuse, which is partly why she hadn't told him.

grounding: Shows a young married couple negotiating shared finances and family duties over a week.

passage:
Aadhya, you asked how your uncle and I decided who does what. Sit, I'll tell you.
When we married, I was twenty-five, a schoolteacher; he was an engineer. Everyone assumed I'd cook, manage the house and his parents' visits, and still teach. For a year, I did. I was so tired I cried in the school staffroom once.
One night I didn't cook. When he came home I said, "I can't do everything and keep my job. We need to divide this like partners, or I'll break."
He was shocked; he hadn't noticed. We wrote a list on the back of a calendar: cooking, bills, cleaning, his parents, my parents. We split it, and swapped some every few months.
Your uncle still makes the Sunday breakfast, thirty years on.
So before you marry, Aadhya, talk about the list. Your Anjali Bua learned it the tired way.

qa.q: Where did they write their list?
qa.a: On the back of a calendar.

qa.q: How did young Anjali feel during the first year of marriage?
qa.a: Young Anjali felt exhausted and overwhelmed, once crying in the school staffroom.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Anjali's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The night she stopped cooking and asked to divide the work like partners mattered, because it led to a shared list they kept revising.

qa.q: How might Anjali's husband have felt when she spoke up that night?
qa.a: Anjali's husband was probably shocked and a bit ashamed at not having noticed, then willing to change.

grounding: Illustrates an elder recounting how she and her husband negotiated roles in their marriage.

passage: They had forty-eight hours to sign the lease on the Kochi flat, and Tanvir and Raghav still hadn't agreed on how to split anything. The broker kept calling. That evening the power went out in Raghav's building, so they sat on the stairs with a torch and a notebook. "I earn more," Raghav said. "I should pay more rent." Tanvir shook his head. "Then I'll feel like a guest." They tried another way: rent in proportion to income, a shared account for groceries and bills, each keeping their own savings. Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it; Tanvir took the laundry and the monthly paperwork. The harder question came last. "Your parents still think I'm your flatmate," Tanvir said quietly. Raghav was silent a while. "I'll tell them before we move. Together, if you'll come." Tanvir squeezed his hand. They signed the next morning.

qa.q: Which chore did Raghav take on?
qa.a: Cooking went to Raghav, who loved it.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir refuse to let Raghav simply pay more rent?
qa.a: Tanvir worried about feeling like a guest instead of an equal partner in their home.

qa.q: What helped them reach a fair arrangement under pressure?
qa.a: They tried a proportional split, a shared account for bills and separate savings, divided chores by preference, and faced the family question openly.

qa.q: What would change if Raghav kept the relationship hidden from his parents?
qa.a: Tanvir would likely keep feeling hurt and unseen in their shared life, and the secret could strain the partnership.

grounding: Shows a young couple negotiating money, chores and honesty with family before moving in together.
